subject: History of USA
title: 8. The United States in the First and Second World Wars

segments.text: Compare 1919 with 1945 directly: after WWI the U.S. rejected League membership and limited long-term European commitment; after WWII it helped design and lead a permanent international order — this contrast is the topic’s central analytical point.

President Wilson initially kept the U.S. neutral while American trade and finance increasingly favoured the Allies; German unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram led the United States to

Interwar neutrality laws reflected many Americans’ belief that entanglement had drawn the country into WWI unnecessarily, but German and Japanese expansion gradually weakened isolationist sentiment; Roosevelt supported Britain through

items.text: The pre-1941 U.S. programme supplying Britain and other Allies with materiel while formally remaining outside the war.
Make a direct WWI-versus-WWII comparison: reason for entry, military role, home front, peace settlement and postwar international commitment.
Do not say the U.S. was economically neutral throughout WWI; trade and finance increasingly connected it to the Allies.
Do not say Senate rejection of Versailles meant complete isolation from world affairs.
Do not treat Pearl Harbor as the only cause of global U.S. involvement; tensions with Japan and support for the Allies had developed earlier.
The U.S. entered WWI in April 1917; the Senate did not consent to Versailles and the U.S. never joined the League.
Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941) brought the U.S. into WWII.
The U.S. used atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
The 1919-versus-1945 contrast (rejecting versus leading a permanent international order) is the topic’s central point and should organise the whole answer.
U.S. involvement in both wars was preceded by substantial economic and political entanglement well before formal entry — neutrality was never absolute in either case.
